sections.topic_sentence: **Engineering.** The discipline of exercising informed *control* over consequential systems and accepting *responsibility* for their outcomes.
One way to understand MAGE—Model-Based Agentic Engineering—is as a classical software-engineering move: **add a level of indirection.**[^indirection]
This book began with one hard engineering problem that emerged over months of building a real production system.
Agents can produce changes much faster than the surrounding environment can understand or govern them.
This book began with DocAble, a production service for remediating inaccessible documents.
MAGE draws on two kinds of evidence.

sections.heading_text: What the method turned out to be
sections.topic_sentence: Two principles organize MAGE:
This book is for software engineers who suspect the ground has moved and want to know where to stand.
Agent products and foundation models will continue to change.[note: Engineering predates machine learning in its use of models as purposeful representations of systems.

points.text: Foundation models and agent products keep changing; the durable engineering problem begins when an agent works autonomously where "it usually works" is not an acceptable standard.

The object of engineering expands beyond the implementation to the environment through which autonomous work proceeds: what the agent can know, what it may do, what evidence it must produce, and which obligations the environment will enforce.

MAGE is principally about that environment; the method lies in the representations agents and engineers reason through, the mechanisms that enforce obligations, and the judgment that decides what should become durable engineering structure.
Modeling and Alignment supply the printer's missing instruction halves.
External representation, memory, and tools have long improved machine reasoning; MAGE changes the engineering object: the engineered environment through which autonomous work proceeds over time.

sections.topic_sentence: The Printer suggests a useful diagnostic rule: suspect the engineered setup before inferring a machine limit.

points.text: The Printer suggests a diagnostic rule: suspect the engineered setup before inferring a machine limit.
A failed part can reveal several different problems.
Inferred completion is not an explicit specification.

When an agent produces the wrong result, inspect first what the engineer controlled — instructions, representation, task boundary, tools, evidence; failed output alone does not establish that the foundation model lacks the capability.
Abundant implementation raises the stakes: capable agents execute a bad direction at extraordinary speed, and velocity amplifies sound engineering and bad engineering alike.

preamble_points.text: Coding agents make implementation cheap enough to change the engineering problem; a sound spec, a useful representation, and evidence do not arrive with that capacity — implementation speed amplifies the engineering around it.
A 3D printer is fabricative (open-ended) productive machinery.
Open-ended capability must itself be engineered to use reliably.
Intent is not the same as fabrication instructions.
As implementation becomes abundant, engineering leverage moves toward the instructions, representations, constraints, evidence, and infrastructure that shape autonomous work.
The governed environment is the printer's engineered instruction set.

points.text: The explicit problem: inaccessible university documents at scale.
One project answered both problems: build the production system, and use the engineering work to discover what sustained agentic development demanded.

sections.topic_sentence: From the user's perspective, DocAble is simple: upload an inaccessible document; receive a remediated document and an evidence record.

points.text: From the user's view DocAble is simple: an inaccessible document goes in; a remediated document and an evidence record come back.
The glimpse stops at the boundary; before looking inside, we need only know what engineering result the system is supposed to produce.
The simple interface hides a large production system.
Eight one-line requirements state what DocAble had to accomplish; they are the specification for the case.
The requirements suffice to understand the examples; the factories chapter returns to them as engineering constraints under delegated implementation.

sections.topic_sentence: Building DocAble well is not one engineering problem.

points.text: Building DocAble well is not one engineering problem; different questions require different representations.
Structure, behavior, decisions, measurement, and provenance are different questions, each wanting its own representation of the same system.

The system has not changed between these questions; the representation has. No single model is best for all of them — each is a purposeful reduction that preserves the facts one question needs and suppresses detail it does not.
That is the modeling move Chapter 2 develops.

sections.topic_sentence: Before Chapters 2 and 3 examine particular properties of DocAble, [ref:one-docable-job] follows one ordinary job through the system.

points.text: Before Chapters 2 and 3 examine particular properties of DocAble, one ordinary job through the system shows what those properties concern.

A job tracks one document's trip; a chunk is a portion of that work processed independently; workers claim chunks, calling specialized services; queues coordinate handoffs; the outputs are the remediated document and its evidence.

The same worker appears differently in later models — a deployable component, an actor in a lifecycle, an owner of a resource, a subject of an access policy, or a source of measurements; not competing descriptions, but different properties of the same system.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble is the book's deepest worked example because the system can be examined at the resolution the method requires.

points.text: DocAble is the book's deepest worked example because its engineering can be shown at the resolution the method requires; Chapter 2 asks which representations make properties tractable, Chapter 3 how intent comes to bind the work.

The interlude after Chapter 3 follows one engineering problem in depth — a large presentation exposes a memory problem, then a representation problem, then an execution problem, and successive models reveal each and support design decisions before the implementation is complete.

Chapter 5 uses DocAble differently: it examines the build itself — what failed, what those failures revealed, and how recurring judgments became models, controls, and other durable engineering structure.

DocAble provides depth, not the book's entire evidentiary basis; other engineering organizations reappear to show where related structures recur, where they take different forms, and where the evidence supports a more limited interpretation.
We can now examine the machinery that makes autonomous implementation possible and the engineering mechanisms through which MAGE acts on it.

preamble_points.text: You will meet DocAble in every section; here is just enough to hold it.

sections.topic_sentence: A foundation model supplies broad semantic reasoning at low marginal cost.

points.text: A foundation model supplies broad inexpensive semantic reasoning; an agentic harness turns it into action, manages the working context, and exposes points where the work can be observed or constrained — the useful unit is the pair inside an engineered environment.
Four properties of the foundation model matter to the engineering argument: broad semantic reasoning, probabilistic output, bounded working state, and cheap repeated reasoning.

The harness contributes three complementary capabilities: action (tools turn outputs into operations), context management (assembling and maintaining working state), and interposition (points where the environment can observe, constrain, or deny an action).

None of these properties is alien to human engineering; what changes is their combination with broad inexpensive reasoning and a machine-mediated environment, and recent harness-engineering work treats autonomous capability as a property of the model–harness–environment system.

sections.topic_sentence: Scale creates a reasoning problem before an agent ever enters the picture.

points.text: Scale creates a reasoning problem before an agent enters; a long engineering task is a sequence of related decisions whose required state grows while the active state available to the reasoner stays finite.

Once a task exceeds active state, some information must live elsewhere and be recovered; poor reconstruction re-solves solved questions and contradicts constraints, so the problem is how much question-relevant state must be reconstructed for the next judgment.

Harnesses move the boundary by expanding or better managing working state, but availability is not a useful representation — usable context falls short of nominal capacity and present state is not equally accessible, and raw implementation is an expensive substrate when the question depends on a smaller set of relationships.

The reasoning horizon is a locality problem: systems keep useful state close to the computation that consumes it, and purposeful representations apply the same principle semantically — a dependency graph or state machine answers a question that retrieved source lines merely make available.

The reasoning horizon is the boundary beyond which consequential state can no longer be carried in active reasoning and must be reconstructed; larger windows, stronger reasoners, retrieval, and memory move it, and Modeling moves it differently by changing the representation over which reasoning occurs.

sections.topic_sentence: The second problem is not that agents make mistakes while human programmers do not.

points.text: Software engineering has always separated authorship from assurance — we compile instead of trusting a prediction, test instead of accepting an explanation — because the producer's confidence is not enough.

Commodity intelligence makes that separation more important because implementation is cheap and repeatable; an agent can propose, inspect, explain, and repair, but another judgment from the same substrate does not constitute independent evidence — the environment must establish what evidence counts.

The consequential judgments that still depend on fallible per-instance inference form the probabilistic surface; better models, context, decomposition, harnesses, and iterative loops make those judgments more reliable but leave the obligation dependent on probabilistic judgment each time it arises.

sections.topic_sentence: Software engineering offers another move.

points.text: For selected obligations the environment can make the required property explicit and enforce it independently of the producing run — represent an architectural restriction and reject changes that violate it — so the judgment that established the obligation is reused across later implementation.

Important changes reach the system through identifiable interfaces — inputs, tool calls, edits, outputs, lifecycle transitions — where a sandbox, hook, or test can act without a rich model, and explicit representations extend the semantic reach of those same control points.

preamble_points.text: Engineering methods fit the substrate they act on; reinforced concrete works because concrete takes compression and steel takes tension, and agentic engineering likewise begins by asking what productive machinery entered the process and which of its properties matter.

The relevant substrate is not a foundation model alone but a foundation model operating through an agentic harness inside an engineered environment; the combination determines both what autonomous work can do and where engineering can act on it.

sections.topic_sentence: The properties of agentic machinery leave two engineering problems.

points.text: The properties of agentic machinery leave two engineering problems: a finite reasoner needs representations that keep relevant state tractable, and fallible autonomous work needs enforcement outside the producing run.

The two problems, related but distinct: the Representation Problem (how to represent a large system so relevant properties are reasoned about without reconstruction) answered by Modeling in Chapter 2, and the Enforcement Problem (how intent comes to bind autonomous work so satisfying obligations does not depend on the producer self-certifying) answered by Alignment in Chapter 3.

Modeling makes selected properties explicit enough to reason about; Alignment enforces selected obligations over realization; neither requires the other in every case, but together they let engineering knowledge and judgment persist outside any one producing run.

sections.heading_text: The Problem Is Larger than Software
sections.topic_sentence: Software makes the problem unusually visible, but does not create it.

points.text: Software makes the governing problem visible; it does not create it.

sections.heading_text: Modeling Is a Classical Engineering Move
sections.topic_sentence: Modeling is not new.

points.text: Modeling is not new: engineering has long used representations that suppress irrelevant detail so a property can be reasoned about directly.

The common move is basic: build a representation in which the property is easier to express, inspect, or analyze than in the realized artifact — useful for what it makes available, not for reproducing the system.

None of these representation forms is new — UML standardized notations for many of them, and requirements engineering long ago externalized goals, assumptions, and specifications; MAGE's claim is not that engineers need a new modeling language.
MAGE adopts this classical move under changed economics: commodity intelligence makes explicit representations cheaper to build and use, and generative implementation makes them more valuable.

For MBSE readers the repertoire is familiar; MAGE's concern is what happens when these representations become part of the engineered environment — agents reason through them, knowledge persists across episodes, and selected properties can become objects of Alignment.

A useful model may be three states and two transitions, a list of permitted edges, or a schema joined on identifiers; the question is never how much can we model, but what representation makes this recurring question easier to answer.

sections.heading_text: A Model Is a Purposeful Reduction
sections.topic_sentence: A **model** is a purposeful reduction of a system.

points.text: A model is a purposeful reduction; its value is what it leaves out. The engineering question decides what to keep.

A representation can contain accurate information and still be inadequate because its output cannot express a consequential case; a DocAble entitlement failure later in the chapter shows a reduction discarding a distinction the code had observed.
Obligations rarely fix one realization; a tolerance bounds permitted variation, a degree of freedom is a choice left open.

sections.topic_sentence: The suppressed detail has a realization-side consequence.

points.text: In software a tolerance can be numeric but is often qualitative, because code owes more to discrete mathematics than to continuous media.

Even a numeric bound is rarely a single line — a budget carries a margin, a capacity envelope leaves headroom — so a quantitative model can represent the band of acceptable variation, not just a target.

Obligations bound the space of acceptable realizations without selecting a point; commodity intelligence makes exercising that freedom cheap, so Modeling names the consequential distinctions and Alignment enforces selected boundaries.
A tacit obligation can look free; the "not that" test reveals a boundary that was never written down.

sections.heading_text: Not every unmodeled choice is free
sections.topic_sentence: This also distinguishes tacit obligations from genuinely free choices.

points.text: Unknown, tacit, explicit, and free are present states of a choice, and they change as the system changes.
Modeling can begin before specification is complete; a reduction can make variation tractable so distinctions can be discovered.
Hold the system constant, change the question, and the model changes; there is no single model of the system.
There is no model of the system, only purposeful reductions that each answer one question.
A model is a reduction first, even when it runs; executability changes what you can DO with it, not whether it abstracts.
Structure — an explicit declared shape a machine can read — is what lets a representation be traversed, checked, and joined.
The simplest useful form of externalized knowledge is a graph of engineering entities and their relations; graph names the structure, not the storage.

Many representations can be read as graphs of entities and relations; shape does not distinguish them, semantics do — a dependency, a transition, an ownership claim, and a permission can all be arrows answering different questions.
Externalized knowledge representation is the lightest form of Modeling, and most of industry already stands on it.

sections.topic_sentence: Structured representations support different capabilities: externalized knowledge, typed relationships, explicit semantics, stated properties, derivation, generation, traceability, and checking.

points.text: Structured representations support different capabilities — externalized knowledge, typed relationships, semantics, properties, derivation, generation, traceability, checking — acquired as engineers ask more, but not a required sequence or maturity model.
Selective modeling: model facts repeatedly reconstructed and properties repeatedly adjudicated, adding structure when the reduction in recurring engineering work justifies carrying it.

Enforcement stays separate: a rich model may remain advisory while permissions, sandboxes, compilers, or tests enforce obligations with little modeling; Modeling expands the set of properties that can be stated and evaluated, and Chapter 3 asks which the engineered environment should enforce.
The classification caveat: six classes organized by the engineering question a model answers, useful rather than exhaustive, and able to overlap.
The six classes differ less in shape than in semantics: each can be understood as a graph of things and relationships, and what changes from class to class is what the nodes and edges mean.

MAGE classifies models by engineering question rather than notation because the same graph-shaped representation can answer very different questions depending on its semantics, and one system fact can participate in several views.

A portion of the established repertoire — nine familiar representations read as a set of moves, not a taxonomy of all modeling; MAGE prescribes no new notation, and the repertoire is larger than the six classes below.

This chapter illustrates modeling practice rather than exhausting it; once the engineering question is known, start with the representations the field has already developed — the repertoire is reusable engineering knowledge, and choosing from it remains engineering judgment.

Telemetry is observation, and a measurement model relates quantities — usage times price is cost, concurrent jobs are capacity demand — so a bound becomes statable; logs and traces are observability, and a provenance model selects and structures realized history so "what changed, and what evidence records it" becomes a query rather than a search.
The classes classify questions, not data structures; one represented fact can answer several. The lease is Ownership, Behavioral, and Measurement at once.
System knowledge is the connected substrate where the six classes meet, not a seventh peer class.
The classes name the engineering question; tolerance names the variation that question permits, not a seventh class.
The model class names the engineering question; the representation form is a separate choice, so purpose comes first and representation follows.

The sections ahead develop three classes in detail through production models from DocAble; the final section asks how such representations connect through shared identity, reaching for measurement and provenance views where the connected substrate needs them.
A model does not govern by existing; modeling makes a property explicit, and Alignment makes selected properties enforceable.

preamble_points.text: A foundation model knows the languages and patterns; it does not know your system — those facts live in the engineered environment.
The first modeling move is simple: externalize engineering knowledge that should not have to be rediscovered.

Natural language is a representation, and often an appropriate one; consequential knowledge kept only in prose must be articulated correctly and then recovered correctly by each later reasoner, and a structured model can preserve distinctions that would otherwise be restated or reconstructed.
The Modeling Principle in its weakest form: externalize engineering knowledge into explicit, structured models to reason through.

sections.heading_text: The Canonical Move: Structure and Dependency
sections.topic_sentence: A component diagram names which services exist; a dependency graph names which modules rest on which; a call graph names which procedures may invoke which; a data-flow diagram names how information moves through transformations; a deployment topology names what is connected across execution locations.

points.text: Component and dependency graphs, call graphs, data-flow diagrams, and deployment topologies all name the entities a question needs and the declared relations between them, and drop the behavior.

A structural model selects the entities a question needs and the relations between them; the edge label is where the engineering meaning lives, so a generic "related-to" edge discards the distinction the model exists to preserve.

Explicit structure turns the claims an engineer wants into graph properties — local, path, or whole-graph — and the analyses into ordinary graph operations: reachability, reverse traversal, cycle detection, impact and conformance.

Static analysis can derive the graph from code and engineers can declare it as intent; one describes what the system appears to do, the other what it is supposed to do, and Chapter 3 treats the difference.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble supports several structured document formats through libraries powerful enough to alter their underlying object structures.

points.text: The model draws one architectural relation — remediation reaches format-specific mutation through a structured-document seam, realized per format — and leaves queues, retries, sessions, and repair mechanics out.
The model states the boundary as a path property — every ordinary mutation route crosses the seam — and exposes it to checking; a static control that flags a bypass is the Chapter 3 enforcement.

A structural model carries the opposite risk — the code moves and the drawing does not — so the boundary it shows quietly stops matching the system; that gap is model drift, and later sections keep the correspondence by deriving, generating, or tracing.

sections.topic_sentence: The document-mutation model asked where one kind of change belongs.

points.text: A second structural question reaches inside remediation: which computations make up the pipeline, and how do they depend on one another; the first reduction treats each registered pass as a node.

DocAble's computation model represents registered computations as nodes and distinguishes a data-flow edge (information consumed to produce a result) from a control edge (information consulted only to decide whether to run).

The same model records how bounded each computation's effect is — a typed patch for all or part of its edits, or a direct in-place edit — exposing distinctions the implementation contains but does not represent uniformly.

The computation model is static per run, but other views attach observations to its stable computation identities — DocAble now joins staged-run latency and cost to those identities without turning the structural graph into an execution log.

Additional engineering views attach by computation identity rather than enlarging the structural schema; declared properties state intent, measured properties report observation, so an unmeasured value is unknown, not zero.

sections.heading_text: The Canonical Move: States, Transitions, and Executions
sections.topic_sentence: Engineering has represented behavior this way for a long time.

points.text: Engineering has long represented behavior as states and transitions — automata, labeled transition systems, statecharts, temporal specifications — all keeping states and transitions and discarding the code that realizes them.
Reducing a service to states and transitions turns "can it reach a state it should never occupy?" from a reconstruction over scattered handlers into a question a person or tool can answer.

A node is a legal state, an edge a permitted transition, a path an admitted execution; the transitions the model omits are the behaviors it declares illegal, and the property's shape selects the checker.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble has one behavioral obligation whose violation is quiet and expensive.

points.text: The recovery obligation lives in the gap between local staging and durable publication: there is no direct FALLBACK_STAGED to DB_UPDATED edge, so the record can never point at a not-yet-durable artifact.

Over the model the obligation is a reachability property — DB_UPDATED is reachable only through FALLBACK_UPLOADED — that the model exposes and a checker can search; whether a transition table refuses the short-circuit is a Chapter 3 question of enforcement.

sections.topic_sentence: The recovery model answers a safety question — can a bad state be reached?

points.text: The recovery model answers a safety question one counterexample settles; "every job eventually terminates" is liveness, ranging over infinite executions, and needs a different checker.
Once behavior is explicit the right reasoning becomes available per property; the three-state recovery ordering is a sharp slice of a fuller job lifecycle chosen for crash-safe publication.

The recovery model makes an ordering obligation explicit and searchable; it does not establish that the implementation realizes it, prove it is the right ordering, or decide the consequence of a violation.

sections.topic_sentence: With one worker, *who owns this job?* has an obvious answer.

points.text: With many workers, a crash, and a reclaim sweep, "who owns this job?" acquires time and contention; engineering's vocabulary of locks, leases, and claims relates a holder to a resource over time, and an ownership model keeps those relationships and discards the rest.

A claim binds a holder to a resource and carries which holder, which generation of claim, and when it expires — the generation being what tells a current claim from a superseded one — and because the hard failures live in interleavings, the characteristic analysis is state-space exploration with invariant checking.

A job is leased exactly when it has an owner; the two are the same fact from two sides, so the model represents ownership as the presence of a current claim — this is what "leased" means, and it sets up the invariant that follows.

Suppose A holds generation 7, stalls, and is reclaimed; the job is re-leased to B at generation 8; a late release from A carrying generation 7 must not clear B's generation-8 claim, and the generation makes that decidable.

The generation makes "is this release applicable to the current claim?" decidable — the property the model exposes; whether a release path compares generations and rejects the stale one is the Chapter 3 enforcement, verified separately by exhaustive interleaving search.
The lease model makes ownership under contention precise and its invariant checkable; it does not establish the implementation obeys the invariant, nor decide what a stale release should trigger.

sections.topic_sentence: The lease is the chapter's clearest case of one representation answering several classes of question.

points.text: Read as ownership the lease says who controls a job; read as behavioral it traces a claimed-held-expired-reclaimed lifecycle; counted, it measures how much work is in flight — one representation, three questions.

That a lease serves ownership, behavioral, and measurement questions at once confirms the §2.1 claim that the classes sort questions, not data structures — the observation the closing section builds on to connect the models.

sections.topic_sentence: Engineering represents permission in several familiar forms: decision tables that map conditions to allowed actions, rule systems, access-control matrices that record which subject may act on which object,[cite: lampson1974] policy graphs, feature models that constrain which combinations of options are valid, and constraint systems that declare which assignments are admissible.

points.text: Decision tables, rule systems, access-control matrices, policy graphs, feature models, and constraint systems all represent permission; what unifies them is not their shape but their normative mood.

A structural edge and a decision edge can be drawn identically and mean opposite kinds of thing — a fact about what happens versus a rule about what is permitted; an absent decision edge means "not allowed," not "does not happen."

Once permission is declared, the claims a policy designer wants become expressible — permitted/forbidden, mutual exclusion, prerequisites, consistency, completeness, least privilege — and "is this allowed?" becomes an evaluation rather than an argument.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble declares which of its services may communicate with which.

points.text: The declared graph is the single source of truth for permitted inter-service edges, with one node declared publicly reachable and every other edge authenticated; a completeness check requires each gated edge to be fully specified, and the deployment config is generated from the graph.
The observed call graph reveals that A calls C; the decision model states whether A may call C; agreement is correspondence, not correctness — a faithfully-obeyed rule can still be the wrong rule.

DocAble generates config from the declared graph but does not reconcile observed traffic against it at runtime; that open correspondence is the cleanest illustration in the chapter of a model exposing a checkable property without, by itself, establishing correspondence.

sections.heading_text: DocAble: When the System Changed but the Model Did Not
sections.topic_sentence: The service-flow policy was declared as intent, ahead of any violation.

points.text: The service-flow policy was declared in advance; DocAble's upload-admission decision acquired its model in the opposite order, after a production failure exposed a representation that could no longer express the decision.
A user receives upload entitlement through groups — finite-credit or unlimited — so the admission decision depends on two facts: how many credits remain and whether any entitlement is unlimited.

DocAble originally had only finite-credit groups, so a scalar sum was an adequate admission representation; when unlimited groups arrived, no explicit model of the admission decision existed to carry the change.

The legacy reduction read each group's unlimited flag and used it to exclude unlimited groups from the credit sum; its scalar output had no place for "unlimited," so an unlimited user became zero credits — a representation failure, not missing information.

The same-day root-cause analysis made the admission question explicit and produced an explicit entitlement decision model — with property tests, a cross-runtime parity corpus, and a shape lint — in roughly five hours from RCA to deletion of the lossy reduction.

The repair changed the representation through which the decision was made, not merely the failing conditional: the revised model preserves the finite/unlimited distinction and states the admission decision explicitly, and the implementation was then changed to consume it.

The failure revealed a decision made through a representation that could no longer express the system's domain; making the decision explicit forced the representation to preserve the distinction the system had acquired.

The author changed the system concept in one place and did not carry it into another representation of the same decision; an explicit model would not have prevented the bug, but it would have made the obligation to update the corresponding representation visible.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble's models differ in shape on purpose.

points.text: DocAble's models differ in shape by design — registries, state machines, contracts, quantitative relations — and share identities and query surfaces rather than one universal representation.
The substrate is layered structured data, deliberately decoupled from the code it describes so the two can be reconciled.
The models cohere semantically, not syntactically: the same entity named in one model resolves to the same entity in another.
Prefer shared identity and derivation over independently maintained copies of the same fact; where duplication is unavoidable, make the correspondence explicit and checkable.
Join static and runtime only when a question pays.

sections.heading_text: What Happened, and What Evidence Records It
sections.topic_sentence: That realized history deserves its own reduction.

points.text: A system may emit millions of events yet leave a consequential question — what changed this artifact, which operation changed it, what evidence supports the account — hard to answer, so a provenance model selects and structures the history that answers it.

Choosing the event grain is part of the modeling decision — too coarse collapses distinct changes into an opaque "document modified" event, too fine becomes another execution trace later reasoning must reconstruct into meaning.

A human-facing explanation is derived from the same structured history rather than maintained as a second, independently-written account; record the consequential action once, then derive the audit, debugging, or changelog view from it.

The recorded history can be replayed: the PDF path records mutations as typed edit values in a per-session log, and a replay engine applies the same sequence deterministically, so one representation both explains and reproduces the resulting mutations while remaining a purposeful reduction of execution.

The computation graph asks what may compose, the provenance record says which mutations did occur in this run, and replay asks whether that history can be reproduced — three separate questions, no one representation subsuming the others.

The model records attribution per mutation; a structural check can establish that every mutator leaves an attribution record but not that the semantic account inside it is correct — this chapter models the evidence, Chapter 3 enforces the obligation.

sections.topic_sentence: A model makes selected properties of a system available for reasoning.

points.text: A model makes selected properties of a system available for reasoning; joining models makes properties that cross those representations available — analogous to the questions integration testing asks that unit testing cannot.

One typed interservice-call edge joins to deployment configuration for the callee URL, to runtime identity for the required invocation grant, and to the service catalog for topology agreement; 28 modeled edges produce 10 distinct grants, a deployment plan no single artifact contains.

Connections can create information that no individual model contains: the call model lacks the environment-specific runtime identity, the deployment environment does not state the intended topology, and their join determines the permission that should exist.

Declared invariant facts derive a verification tier, the tier mandates a checker kind, and a check joins the citation against the checker corpus on disk — so a declared property can determine what kind of evidence must exist.
Each representation can be locally reasonable while their composition fails to preserve a distinction the engineering decision requires — the entitlement failure crossed exactly such a seam.
Semantic unity lets an agent enter the substrate at the entity its task names and follow relations outward, taking only the connected slice the question needs.

sections.topic_sentence: Multiple models create a correspondence problem: represented facts can diverge from the system or from one another.

points.text: A family of models invites an obvious danger — a second system of record that quietly diverges from the first — and the answer is to engineer the relationship between map and territory, not to stop modeling.
A model and the code stay equal by derivation, and derivation runs in one of two directions; the machinery that keeps them equal depends on which.

sections.heading_text: Derive when implementation owns the truth
sections.topic_sentence: The model is a projection of the code, reconciled at build time.

points.text: The remediation subsystem now illustrates both directions around one source of truth: its explicit computation model is consumed by execution, so realization follows the model rather than reconstructing composition from node implementations — the generate case.
A separate Python remediation-graph view projects that structure for analysis and governance — queryable, joinable, drift-checked — without becoming the runtime scheduler.

One source of truth supports both directions at once: execution consumes the authoritative model while analytical views derive from it or from parity-bound declarations; the question is which representation owns the fact and which consumers must follow it.
Derivation settles correspondence, not whether the architecture is good.
Where neither side can be fully derived from the other, maintain traceability between them and check the predicates that are mechanically decidable.

sections.heading_text: Trace and check where neither owns the truth
sections.topic_sentence: Where neither side can be fully derived from the other, the move is **traceability plus drift checking**.

points.text: Mechanical correspondence has a declared surface: some claims are decidable, others remain semantic and require judgment, and still others are not modeled at all.

sections.topic_sentence: Mechanical correspondence has a declared surface.

points.text: Two different gaps: a semantic miss, where correspondence still holds syntactically but meaning has changed, and an unmodeled region, which has no model-based coverage.
Operationally, an executable model is its structured schema plus the predicates a machine can check over that schema; a schema without checked predicates is only half the pattern.
Synchronization does not establish that the model is correct; a model can be perfectly in sync and still express the wrong architecture.
The bounded guarantee — decide the decidable over the claimed surface — is the boundary Chapter 3 opens on, where agreement is distinguished from correctness.

sections.heading_text: Modeling Makes Properties Available to Engineering
sections.topic_sentence: A model does not govern the system merely by existing.

points.text: A model does not govern by existing: a structural model names a forbidden dependency without preventing it, a behavioral model an illegal transition without rejecting it, a measurement model a budget without stopping work — Modeling makes the property explicit, it does not enforce it.

DocAble's cost-and-capacity model relates usage and pricing to an attributable cost against a budget and concurrency to a capacity demand against an envelope, and attaches no hard invariant to either quantity: the model says cost can be compared against a budget, not that it must not exceed one.

The cost-and-capacity model makes spending attributable and demand comparable to an envelope; it does not decide the budget, guarantee the numbers are collected correctly, or enforce the bound — a model earning its place by exposing a property while leaving enforcement open.

Local syntactic obligations need little modeling; architectural boundaries, temporal obligations, distributed ownership, provenance, and end-to-end policy need enough representation to expose the relevant relationships, which Modeling makes available to analysis and governance.

Alignment does not require a separately represented model — some obligations are observable at an action or artifact boundary and can be constrained directly; models extend the range of properties the environment can enforce.

DocAble's models arose around engineering questions that implementation alone made expensive, ambiguous, or unsafe to reconstruct; across the cases, the useful model is the representation that preserves the distinctions and relationships a consequential question requires.
Chapter 3 asks which obligations the engineered environment should enforce, where they become decidable, and what evidence and mechanisms are sufficient to enforce them.
Models can provide value before enforcement — reasoning, analysis, composition, traceability — and Chapter 3 asks the separate question of enforcement.

preamble_points.text: The worked examples are not fragments of one universal model; they are a family of structured models joined where useful. System knowledge is the substrate that connects them, not a seventh class.

sections.heading_text: Reasoning Input, Action, Work Unit, and Artifact/Runtime
sections.topic_sentence: The first location is **reasoning input**: the context, representations, examples, and instructions put in front of the reasoner.

points.text: The first location is reasoning input: ordinarily guidance, not enforcement.
The first enforcement boundary is the action: one attempted side effect the harness can inspect or refuse.
The second enforcement boundary is the work unit, where whole-work obligations become legible.
The third enforcement boundary is the artifact or runtime: forbidden state made impossible to express or accept.

sections.heading_text: Placement and Strength Are Different Decisions
sections.topic_sentence: The four boundaries do not form a monotonic scale from weak to strong.

points.text: The four boundaries do not form a monotonic weak-to-strong scale.
Substantial enforcement can exist without rich models; richer models expand the properties the environment can state and govern.

sections.heading_text: Return Evidence at the Earliest Useful Boundary
sections.topic_sentence: The boundaries also decide where feedback can return.

points.text: Every boundary also determines where feedback can return; earlier evidence means less to reconstruct.
These mechanisms do not act independently; the interplay is its own problem, deferred to §3.5.
The Alignment Principle, stated whole: make engineering obligations enforceable by encoding them into mechanisms — constrain, sense, evaluate, admit — that can enforce them.
Enforcement installed at a boundary is easiest to see in systems already using it.

preamble_points.text: The environment intervenes between a proposed action and its consequence.
Guidance influences behavior; enforcement determines what the environment permits or accepts, and feedback returns evidence between them.
Recent agentic-security guidance draws a similar boundary: secure the process that produces the artifact.
An obligation can be enforced at several boundaries; choose where it is visible and a mechanism can enforce it.

sections.topic_sentence: A drift check can establish a declared correspondence between two artifacts.

points.text: A drift check establishes agreement between two artifacts, not that the correspondence expresses the right intent.
The distinction is not derived versus authored; it is description versus independent obligation.
Drift checking has a precise job: preserve a declared correspondence between model and implementation; correctness needs another claim.
Three different relations matter — correspondence, conformance, or acceptance — and they are not interchangeable.

sections.topic_sentence: A second problem is placement.

points.text: An obligation can be stated clearly and still be unenforceable at the boundary where you try to check it.
A deployment can pass every earlier check and still serve a blank page; the property is legible only once the pieces compose in the served system.
Checking model drift at the commit is the wrong granularity; the property belongs to the completed unit of work.

sections.topic_sentence: The agent-return check is one instance of a rule that runs under the whole of this chapter:

points.text: The design rule: place enforcement at the earliest boundary where the obligation is both legible and decidable.
The rhyme: Modeling chooses the reduction that answers the question without carrying unnecessary detail; Alignment chooses the earliest boundary where the obligation is legible.
Real boundaries are sometimes approximate: semantic placement is an engineering trade-off, not a demand for a theoretically perfect hook.
The section has supplied both requirements for enforcement; the next question is what the mechanism at that boundary actually does.

preamble_points.text: Enforcement needs an obligation independent of the work being judged, and a boundary at which that obligation is legible.
An obligation may live in a model, or directly in a type, permission, schema, test, or policy; Alignment does not require a particular representation.

Software engineering already connects intent to realization through requirements, traceability, verification, and acceptance; Alignment builds on that tradition but adds a further question — should the resulting judgment merely inform the work, or should the environment enforce it?

Traceability can relate an obligation, its realization, and its evidence without any mechanism enforcing the obligation — a requirement can trace cleanly to a test whose failure is merely reported, and a permission boundary can enforce firmly without a rich traceability model.
Where an obligation permits variation, the acceptable region must come from governing intent, not from the realization being judged.
Two lessons: agreement is not correctness, and placement must follow the meaning of the obligation.

sections.topic_sentence: On the work-facing side of the loop, the two complementary moves are prevention and observation; [ref:constraint-vs-sensor] draws the split.

points.text: On the work-facing side of the loop, the two moves are prevention and observation.
An instruction is enforced only when a mechanism in the environment acts on it.
A sensor observes and produces evidence — actual = observe(system); it does not judge, and acting on it costs an iteration.
A CI suite bundles sensor, validator, and gate without collapsing the distinction among them.
A sensor is only as good as its observability — the semantic gap from the other side.
A constraint prevents drift within the iteration, costing none.
Constraint and sensor echo control engineering — analogy, not identity.
Human process instantiates the same roles: logging senses, the reviewer validates, the approver gates.
The sharpest instance of the pair is ownership: the lease makes ownership visible and recoverable, the durable compare-and-set supplies the constraint. Recovery is not permission.

sections.heading_text: One Obligation, Several Ways to Hold It
sections.topic_sentence: A modeled obligation does not imply one particular enforcement technology.

points.text: A modeled obligation does not imply one enforcement technology; ask what kind of property it is.
If an invalid state can be removed from the action space, prefer the constraint.
Properties that live across sequences need a validator that reasons over the composed state space.
Temporal obligations require another shape of evidence; a finite trace cannot establish eventuality.
These are matches between property and mechanism, not levels of sophistication.
Whichever validator supplies the judgment, the enforcement still depends on what the environment does with its verdict.

sections.topic_sentence: The other two roles act on evidence and admission.

points.text: A validator turns evidence into a judgment.
A gate enforces the verdict — and a gate is a commitment.
A loop may re-derive evidence at a later admission boundary; the thing asking to pass does not define passing.

sections.topic_sentence: The four roles are not stages of maturity.

points.text: The four roles are not stages of maturity: one quantitative model can support observation, adaptation, graceful degradation, or hard admission control.
A quantitative tolerance can expose margin — the room between the realized value and its bound; two conforming realizations can differ in how much room they keep.
Margin is computable only where the model supplies a meaningful distance; many software obligations are qualitative and admit none.

sections.topic_sentence: Constraints are often introduced as prohibitions: this code must not call that library.

points.text: A constraint can forbid an action or require an evidence-producing one; provenance shows the positive form.

sections.topic_sentence: Earlier in this chapter, architectural conformance provided one example of enforcing intended relations.

points.text: Provenance is useful for a particular architectural-conformance problem: the required relation is the path through which a protected operation was derived, not merely which components interact.
Where a consequential effect passes through a recognizable primitive, restrict that surface directly — the prohibited interaction has a tractable signature.
Some obligations have no single forbidden call; a protected operation is reachable by composing otherwise legitimate APIs into a new path.
Provenance reverses enforcement: require the protected operation to carry evidence that it passed through the sanctioned abstraction.
Restrict a small recognizable surface directly; reach for provenance when the obligation concerns how an ordinary operation was derived and its paths are numerous or compositional.
Provenance here is not attribution; it makes a derivation path the sanctioned route to admission — producer-side rules check known emitters, the consumer boundary refuses unknown routes.

sections.topic_sentence: Keep **policy**, **guidance**, and **governance mechanism** separate.

points.text: Keep policy, guidance, and governance mechanism separate; enforcement begins when something acts.
The same artifact can play several roles; the model is the representation, the machinery the enforcement.
Implementations bundle roles; name them, don't stretch the terms.
Leave-with: intent becomes enforceable through one of four roles; next, where the mechanisms come from.

preamble_points.text: Four roles — constrain, sense, validate, gate — separate prevention, observation, judgment, admission.
Two roles act on the work; two act at the door it must pass.

sections.heading_text: Ex Ante: Encode What You Already Know
sections.topic_sentence: Start with obligations you can state before the work begins and that are consequential, recurrent, or reusable enough to make durable.

points.text: Ex ante: encode the obligations you can state up front, and stop paying judgment for them.

sections.heading_text: Ex Post: Convert What the Work Teaches
sections.topic_sentence: The harder half begins when the system surprises you.

points.text: Ex post: diagnose what was missing; not every failure calls for another gate.
The conversion lands in one of five places: model, invariant, sensor, validator, or enforcement.
Alignment failures expose tacit knowledge or obligations that Modeling can externalize.

sections.topic_sentence: A merge automation drained a backlog of agent worktrees into the mainline each tick.

points.text: Governance conversion can add a mechanism; it can also delete a capability the environment should never have offered.

sections.topic_sentence: Governance conversion motivates a useful accounting concept: **engineering capital**.

points.text: Governance conversion forms engineering capital — the concrete positive stock software engineering has lacked a name for.
The asset is not "the team learned" — it is something you can point at.
Capital earns a return: lower marginal engineering cost. Conversion is capital formation.
Capital depreciates; maintenance, reconciliation, and retirement manage it, so accumulation cannot be the objective.
Technical debt and engineering capital are symmetric stocks — both accumulate, both change the economics of later change, both compound.

sections.topic_sentence: Not every quality goal should end in enforcement.

points.text: Where a goal lands turns on three questions; the first is whether the obligation is explicit in a form the environment can use.
The residual is an obligation nobody made explicit enough for the environment to use.
An explicit obligation may still resist cheap mechanical evaluation — an honest boundary, not failed Alignment.
Evaluated only: explicit and evaluated, yet un-gated — because a gate is a commitment.
A governed obligation is enforced in a form appropriate to the engineering decision; the four states are a design space, not a ladder.
Making a tolerance explicit does not mean tightening it; stronger Alignment means dependable enforcement of the obligation engineering chose, not a narrower acceptable set.
An obligation can stop short of a gate for three different reasons; non-enforcement is sometimes the engineered result.
The mechanism that discovers an obligation need not be the one that ultimately enforces it; Chapter 4 follows that migration.
The point is not to drive every obligation to the rightmost leaf; it is to know where each sits and why — and conversion has now created an estate to govern.

preamble_points.text: A governed environment grows ex ante and ex post; governance conversion is the ex post route.

sections.topic_sentence: Start by giving each control a stable identity: the event or boundary at which it acts, the resources it reads or changes, the obligation or failure class that justifies it, and its governance role or roles.

points.text: Catalogue each control: a stable identity, the boundary it acts at, the resources it touches, the obligation it serves, and its governance role.
A catalogue alone cannot tell you whether two sensible controls conflict, nor whether an important obligation has no control; those are relational questions.

sections.topic_sentence: Two collisions from the case study make it concrete.

points.text: A collision lives between two controls, drawn nowhere until the graph draws it.
The interaction graph uses controls as nodes and shared resources as the principal join key; controls need not call one another to collide.
DocAble's implemented governance graph is intentionally partial — a small high-value slice of the larger machinery, not comprehensive coverage.
Shared resource is a useful conservative relation, not a proof that the graph captured every interaction.
Some candidate conflicts are mechanically decidable; others are semantic — a sensor produces evidence of the interaction, a validator or human judges whether it is a conflict.

sections.topic_sentence: Interactions are only half of governing the control machinery.

points.text: A catalogue says what exists and a graph says where controls collide; neither says what should be governed but is not.
Coverage is a small requirements-traceability problem: an obligation with no adequate mechanism is a coverage gap; a mechanism with no obligation is an orphan.
A coverage gap is an uncovered obligation; an orphan is a mechanism with no current purpose. Neither is automatically bad — an orphan is a finding to reconcile, not proof to delete.

sections.topic_sentence: Governance conversion and coverage auditing provide complementary pressures.

points.text: Governance conversion is reactive and coverage auditing is proactive; a healthy environment needs both.
The same audit pushes against permanent accumulation: engineering capital is not the number of controls.
Where DocAble models controls explicitly, entries can be anchored to their implementations and drift-checked, so a mis-placed control fails loud.
Stop the recursion unless experience earns more: a governance model can itself become bureaucracy.

preamble_points.text: Every control can be reasonable in isolation while the control machinery as a whole remains inconsistent, incomplete, or obsolete.
Governance conversion and ex ante design accumulate control machinery; that machinery becomes an engineering object to maintain, reconcile, and sometimes retire.
Alignment turned on itself: a model of the controls, enforced on the controls.

sections.topic_sentence: The Alignment side of [ref:engineer-agent-interaction] contains two distinct activities.
The first models brought into governance should protect the properties that subsequent transformations must not be allowed to damage.
Incremental adoption is easiest to see in a brownfield system.

points.text: The improvement loop has familiar ancestors; the changed condition is implementation abundance.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble originally treated an entire document as one unit of execution.

sections.heading_text: Pages as the Unit of Scale
sections.topic_sentence: As documents grew larger, whole-document execution put increasing pressure on worker memory.
A 250 MB PowerPoint file does not imply that remediation needs 250 MB of document content resident in memory.

sections.heading_text: Remove Media from the Working Set
sections.topic_sentence: The memory problem came from coupling document structure to media residency: total media size increased the worker's persistent working set even though most remediation operations needed only the document's structural skeleton.

sections.heading_text: Once Memory Is Solved, Why Are We Chunking?
sections.topic_sentence: Page chunking had served two roles at once: it partitioned execution and bounded each worker's memory.
Representing remediation as a dependency graph does more than provide an execution plan.
The same analysis exposed a problem in contextual image description (panel c).
The same graph supports a first-order latency model.

sections.heading_text: Predicting the cost of a design change
sections.topic_sentence: Models can also answer questions about designs that do not exist yet.
Implementation eventually supplies measurements, and the useful comparison is not simply whether the result was fast.
The large-file requirement did not produce one model.
The memory story shows the progression clearly:
Laid out this way, the sequence looks like a substantial architecture project.

sections.heading_text: From a Story to a Method
sections.topic_sentence: Nobody began this work with a plan to construct seven models.

sections.heading_text: Start from the System You Own
sections.topic_sentence: Most readers do not begin on a blank page.
Begin with two questions, because representation and enforcement are different things.

sections.heading_text: Reconcile the Map and the Territory
sections.topic_sentence: A recovered representation is a hypothesis.
Brownfield MAGE is not a project to model everything.

sections.heading_text: The GEE as a Distributed Cognitive System
sections.topic_sentence: Not every important judgment should become deterministic.

sections.heading_text: Validate the Change, Not the Producer's Story
sections.topic_sentence: Every engineering process eventually asks the same question: **what evidence is sufficient to accept this change?** Code review, testing, static analysis, operational measurement, and expert judgment answered that question long before coding agents arrived.
The governed engineering environment is itself a consequential system.
This chapter has now shown accumulation three times over: models entering governance, mechanisms preserving what alignment established, recovered structure joining the environment.
One kind of engineering capital remains.
Strip away DocAble, the companion repository, and the current generation of agent harnesses, and a small set of moves remains from this chapter's dynamics and practice.
Before industrial precision, skilled craftspeople could make complicated mechanisms by fitting individual pieces to one another.

points.text: Craft production worked while fabrication knowledge resided in the craftsperson and each artifact was individually reconciled.
Watt's separate condenser was sound as a design, but no workshop could bore a cylinder true enough to realize it.
Wilkinson's boring machinery, built for cannon, changed what could be reliably realized and made Watt's design achievable.
The episode separates design from realization, design capability from production capability, craft knowledge from externalized specification.

sections.topic_sentence: Follow precision one step further and it becomes a form of representation.

points.text: A tolerance is a model of what matters about a part for a particular purpose — a purposeful reduction, not a complete description.

sections.topic_sentence: One precise cylinder is not yet production.

points.text: One precise part is not yet production; repeatable production required parts made independently to correspond to a shared specification.
Whitney's 1801 interchangeability demonstration was staged; the claim preceded, by decades, the production system that could make it true.
Real interchangeability came from decades of armory practice: model artifacts, drawings, gauges, fixtures, and inspection shared across shops.
The drawing states what matters; the gauge gives the statement consequences — representation and enforcement arrived as a pair, and neither suffices alone.
The significance of interchangeable parts is that independently made parts participate in a common system because consequential properties are explicit and repeatable.
Mature industrial production required surrounding machinery: representations, measurement, tooling, process structure, and oversight.
As fabrication scaled, engineering moved consequential knowledge out of the individual fabricator and into the production system.

sections.heading_text: The Supervisor Does Not Watch the Machine
sections.topic_sentence: Interchangeable manufacture succeeded, and its success produced the third failure.

points.text: Steam power increased the capacity of the fabricator; precision manufacturing created a corresponding problem of control that examining every artifact could not answer.

Mature factories learned that the quality team cannot simply examine every widget; tolerances and metrology are central, and the rest of the production system is organized to keep production within tolerance.
A supervisor stays in control through the factory's supervisory surfaces — plans, production state, measurements, alarms, exceptions — not by watching every machine cycle.
A recurring defect changes the factory itself — fixture, tolerance, process, inspection regime, tooling, training, or design — not merely the defective artifact.

sections.topic_sentence: Software largely skipped this separation, because its engineers were also its fabricators.

points.text: Software largely skipped this separation because its engineers were also its fabricators; source code stayed rich because its author was also its interpreter.
Software built pieces of a factory — compiler, build, tests, source control, CI, deployment, observability — while consequential knowledge stayed in human cognition or in the implementation.
Agents break the coupling: software has acquired the equivalent of extremely fast automated machine tools while its supervisory practice still assumes an engineer reads the fabricated artifact.
Making the agent ten times faster does not make artifact-attached supervision more capable; it produces ten times more of the thing supervision must read.

sections.topic_sentence: Only now, with the history in place, name the method.

points.text: Read against the factory's history, the method of the earlier chapters describes components of an industrial production system.
MAGE does not replace the software factory; it supplies representations and supervisory mechanisms through which engineers exercise informed control over automated realization.
Agentic names who performs realization; the supervisory machinery around that realization remains part of the factory.
The software factory's supervisory layer is functional, not a separate technology stack; one artifact can participate in production and in supervision at once.
The industrial history is grounding, not evidence for MAGE: it supplies the shape of the transition, and the warning that the solution was never merely a faster fabricator.
The problem the evidence must answer: increasing the capacity of the fabricator does not necessarily increase the capacity of the supervisor.

preamble_points.text: The printer analogy explained the fabricator; it does not explain mass production through fabricators — for that we need the factory.
Mechanical engineers confronted fabrication outrunning supervision long before software did, and answered with tolerances, metrology, interchangeable manufacture, and process control.
Increasing fabrication capacity changed what the factory itself had to know and enforce, not merely how fast it ran.
The chapter reads the history as three productive failures — capability arriving before the representation and control needed to supervise it — not as a tour of progress.

sections.heading_text: The Problem the Factory Was Built For
sections.topic_sentence: Before the case can carry much weight, the bar has to be clear.

points.text: The problem comes first; it sets the bar the system had to clear.
Title II now governs a university's digital communication, and the 2024 DOJ rule made access part of the service.
Remediating documents by hand costs weeks of specialized work per course, and no manual path scaled.
A document is a visual and semantic artifact.
VLMs changed the feasible boundary; the missing work was the engineering around the model.

sections.topic_sentence: The project began in a committee meeting about the very deadline described above.

points.text: A five-minute feasibility probe proved one component; an agent fleet was put on everything else.
A fleet produced more code than any human could read.
The build moved through seven retrospective stages, each answering a concrete pressure.

sections.topic_sentence: The growing engineered environment is visible in one especially easy-to-count class of artifacts: project-specific lints and gate scripts.

points.text: The control count is evidence of investment, not quality.

sections.topic_sentence: Another coarse measure shows where the engineering effort accumulated.

points.text: Support apparatus outgrew the production code, settling a little above three-to-one.
DocAble did not solve abundant implementation by reading faster; it changed what the engineer had to supervise.

sections.topic_sentence: Start with what the factory knows.

points.text: At the repository revision examined here, DocAble contained 129 declared system models; the exact inventory changes with the system.

The model population is genuinely heterogeneous — registries, instruments, budgets, schemas, constraint sets, dataflows, topologies, state machines, decision tables, policies — split across product-facing and fleet-facing concerns.

Six specimens show the census's purpose: each representation answers an engineering question for a consumer, and its supervisory consequence is what the engineer no longer reconstructs from implementation.
The recurring pattern: each representation replaces implementation-reading with a purpose-built supervisory surface — the supervisor is not supervising two million lines through two million lines.

sections.heading_text: What the Factory Can Derive and Enforce
sections.topic_sentence: A repository can contain excellent documentation and still supervise nothing.

points.text: Models alone would be documentation; the factory joins them and gives them consequences, which is the difference between describing knowledge and acting on it.

The invariant chain: property facts on each invariant derive a verification tier, the tier mandates a checker class, and a check fails when the checker is missing — the model tells the factory what evidence it owes.
The IAM join: service relationships × deployment wiring × runtime identity derive the invoker-grant plan, and a coherence gate asserts the derived grants at deploy time.
The provenance join: every mutation stamps its verb and pass, the customer changelog is derived from the stamps, and a wiring validator catches mutating paths that fail to stamp.

sections.heading_text: The Computation Graph: a Representation That Took Over Execution
sections.topic_sentence: The deepest of the factory's joins earned its position over time, and its history is worth a short telling because a later subsection depends on it.

points.text: The remediation core was decomposed into passes early; their composition stayed implicit until it accumulated global cost.
Deriving the missing composition exposed distinctions the code had never stated: data flow versus control gating, and the boundedness of each pass's mutations.
The pass declarations became the source the graph projects from, a blocking parity check holds them together, and a later redesign made the modeled dependencies authoritative for execution order.

Explicit lifecycle and ownership models made previously slippery properties checkable — exhaustive exploration of the ownership state space, temporal specifications checked mechanically — and created the correspondence obligation in return.

sections.topic_sentence: Where did all this factory machinery come from?

points.text: Where did the machinery come from? Not grand design: governance conversion claims some episodes leave durable structure later work inherits, and this subsection reconstructs the episodes where that sequence is visible.
An implicit lifecycle and a retry reflex became an explicit lifecycle model, atomic claiming, and recovery as a decision over evidence.

A convenient library call that silently destroyed accessibility structure became a canonical-library policy, a typed mutation seam, and a build-time ban — and the gate itself later had to be hardened.

A file path sent across a service boundary became a typed client that makes the mistake unrepresentable, plus an explicit service graph — and a review found the bypass path the boundary did not govern.
"Use types," satisfied to the letter and voided in spirit, became a commodity-lint floor driven to zero plus induced typed abstractions region by region.
Weeks of in-frame autoscaler optimization against the same ceiling became a decision rule: price the architectural change instead of commissioning another local optimization.
A conflict handler with an unmade design decision silently deleted landed work for four days; the choice was made once, encoded, and the destructive default barred.
Two green reports — a lint gate swallowing its own error, pin tests landed onto a tree missing the checked field — became independent evidence regenerated at the admission boundary.
A content-free image detector, provably safe on the world it was measured on, would silence a Rothko; the cheap proxy lost the last word and a regression preserved the failure class.
Eleven mutation sites bypassing the stamp helper shipped blank changelogs; representation, migration, then gating turned provenance from inference into a lookup.
A silent eight-minute stall became a provisional per-chunk worst-case model that is deliberately NOT a gate — alignment need not culminate in blocking enforcement.
Some conversions were mechanical: a repeated review finding — a missing reserved prefix on inserted artifacts — became a blocking lint.
Not every structure was forced by failure: the reactive backend, the closed edit vocabulary, and the unified rule engine were designed from known obligations and simply held.

sections.topic_sentence: What was the human doing while the factory accumulated?

points.text: The five rung labels — co-coder, QA, review lead, tech lead, architect — are retrospective names for the changing center of gravity of the engineer's own work.
Each rung delegated what the environment had just become able to carry: reading, then evaluation, then decidable findings, then locality of reasoning, then system-level knowledge itself.

The staircase's two supports: Alignment moved enforcement of repeatable obligations out of direct review; Modeling moved system knowledge out of the engineer's head; weakness in either sent the work back down.
Interpreted functionally, human attention moved away from supervising individual acts of realization and toward the work only judgment can do.
The payoff: MAGE afforded supervision by changing the objects through which supervision occurred — it did not automate supervision, and human judgment remains central.

sections.heading_text: The Factory Is Also a Liability
sections.topic_sentence: Keeping the case honest requires the other ledger column, because everything this section has praised also has a failure mode.

points.text: A model kept naming a moved symbol and stayed authoritative-looking for days — accumulated structure fails in its own ways.
The liability list: models drift, controls conflict, evidence goes stale, gates encode obsolete assumptions, support machinery needs operating, and engineering capital depreciates.
The claim stays bounded: one longitudinal case, one primary engineer, one model ecosystem, no controlled comparison — the case establishes mechanism and sequence, not prevalence.
The transition: DocAble is one deliberately engineered response to abundant realization; the stronger question is whether independently developed factories exhibit the same pressures.

preamble_points.text: The section opens one deliberately engineered software factory and asks what made it supervisable as its fabrication capacity grew.

sections.topic_sentence: Uber gives the fullest account of realization increasing at organizational scale: more than 70 percent of pull requests attributed to local or cloud agents, more than 3,600 engineer-created agent skills executing over 30,000 times per day, managed agents performing code review, CI repair, end-to-end changes, alert triage, debugging, and maintenance.[cite: medisetty2026factory] What new work inherits is the interesting structure: real workloads become benchmarks; models are selected against cost, quality, and reliability; context and tool access are compiled down to reduce unnecessary reasoning; recurring workflows harden into reusable skills — in one example, deterministic tool orchestration moves out of repeated model turns into executable code, cutting token use by more than half on common workflows and by more than 90 percent in bulk cases.[cite: medisetty2026factory] Supervision is structured by measurement: managed agents are evaluated in units such as cost per merged pull request, review, or alert.

points.text: Uber's realization increase is organization-wide, and the environment around the agents is itself the engineered object: benchmarks, model selection, compiled context, reusable skills, cost-per-outcome.

sections.topic_sentence: GitLab starts from the other end: as code becomes abundant, the scarce problem shifts to trusting it.

points.text: GitLab starts from trust in abundant code and wraps the model in a durable layer — context, verification, governance, identity, provenance — kept independent of any one reasoner.

sections.topic_sentence: Cloudflare gives the cleanest policy-first entry.

points.text: Cloudflare externalizes a standards corpus into machine-readable requirements — mechanically checkable obligations become custom checks, ambiguous ones remain review questions — modeling obligations, not the governed software.

sections.topic_sentence: Siemens enters from outside software-first engineering, and that is exactly its value.

points.text: Siemens, from a model-first engineering tradition, keeps behavioral structure, requirements, simulation, and traceability in persistent representations with software generation downstream — proof the strong end of Modeling is ordinary practice elsewhere.

sections.topic_sentence: Docker's system separates delegated roles, tool permissions, implementation, and evaluation: seven permission-backed roles, an independent reviewer running on a separate model invocation, and deterministic tests supplying repeatable evidence.[cite: delapena2026fleet] Realization and evaluation are both substantially mechanized; final admission deliberately is not.

points.text: Docker separates permission-backed roles, an independent reviewer on a separate model invocation, and deterministic tests — and deliberately keeps final admission human.

sections.topic_sentence: Spotify's Honk system moves large-scale code migration from distributed manual implementation toward centrally scoped, fleet-executed work: a migration that could previously involve hundreds of teams over weeks can be scoped by one engineer over a few days, with tooling identifying and scheduling targets, agents executing changes concurrently, and the engineer supervising the fleet and handling exceptions.[cite: spotify2026honk] The inheritance is the estate representation — a system model and service catalog carrying identities, ownership, dependencies, and lineage — through which migrations are targeted rather than rediscovered per repository.

points.text: Spotify's Honk moves fleet-scale migration from distributed manual work to centrally scoped agent execution over an estate model — one engineer scopes, a fleet implements, supervision handles exceptions.

sections.topic_sentence: Shopify's account describes agent work occurring in shared, observable channels rather than private sessions — one month's snapshot counts 59,918 sessions across 5,170 channels involving more than 7,000 people, "multiplayer by construction."[cite: moreno2026river] Shared sessions become searchable organizational artifacts; recurring knowledge is extracted into skills, conventions, and defaults later agents retrieve.

points.text: Shopify makes agent work multiplayer by construction — tens of thousands of shared sessions become searchable artifacts from which skills and defaults are extracted — a soft externalization with supervision still centered on people.

sections.topic_sentence: Zenseact, building driver-assistance software, describes an organizational split: a platform team owns common substrate — authentication, sessions, execution, and the safety envelope — while domain teams retain their own agents, tools, instructions, and expertise.[cite: dufwa2026zap] Routing machinery selects task-relevant expertise instead of loading the whole organizational corpus into every reasoning window.

points.text: Zenseact centralizes shared substrate — authentication, execution, safety envelope — in a platform team while domain teams keep their own agents and expertise, with routing machinery selecting task-relevant context.

sections.heading_text: What the Factories Share, and Where They Differ
